introduction-why-we-dont-type-ip-address.core: DNS is the internet's distributed phone book: it maps human-friendly names to IP addresses and other data. It's hierarchical (root → TLD → domain), distributed (each zone's owner runs authoritative servers), and heavily cached, so it scales to billions of lookups. It also decouples names from addresses, so servers can move without anyone changing what they type.

first_principles.problem: Users bookmark an IP address and break when the service moves to a new server.

analogy.title: Contacts on your phone
analogy.story: You tap 'Mum'; the phone looks up the number, which can change without you noticing.
analogy.breaks: Your contacts are local; DNS is a global, delegated system.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Name resolved; IP can change behind it.

check.q: What key benefit does DNS give besides convenience?
check.a: Indirection: services can change IP addresses without clients changing anything.

how-a-dns-query-actually-works-the-resol.core: Your device asks a recursive resolver (ISP, 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1 or a VPC resolver). On a cache miss, the resolver walks the hierarchy: it asks a root server, which refers it to the .com TLD servers, which refer it to the domain's authoritative servers, which return the answer. The resolver caches every step by TTL and replies to the client. Most queries are answered from cache.

first_principles.problem: An engineer can't explain why one user sees the new IP and another the old one.
truths: Resolvers do the work for clients.
Each level refers to the next.

analogy.title: Asking a librarian for a rare book
analogy.story: They check their shelf, then the national catalogue, then the regional library, then the specific branch, and remember the location for next time.
analogy.breaks: Librarians remember forever; resolvers forget at TTL expiry.

code.text:
dig +trace www.example.com
# .  NS a.root-servers.net
# com. NS a.gtld-servers.net
# example.com. NS a.iana-servers.net
# www.example.com. A 93.184.215.14

check.q: Why might two users see different IPs for the same name after a change?
check.a: They use different recursive resolvers with different cached records that expire at different times.

the-basic-records-a-aaaa-and-cname.core: An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address and an AAAA record to IPv6; several records give simple round-robin. A CNAME makes one name an alias of another, so the resolver restarts the lookup at the target. A CNAME can't coexist with other records at the same name, so it can't be used at the zone apex, which is why providers offer ALIAS/ANAME or Route 53 alias records.

first_principles.problem: Trying to CNAME example.com to a load balancer hostname fails because the apex also needs NS and SOA records.
truths: CNAME excludes other records at that name.
derivation: Use **ALIAS/alias records** for apex to LB/CDN.

analogy.title: A phone number vs 'call reception instead'
analogy.story: A record is a direct number; CNAME says 'look up this other contact'.
analogy.breaks: Phones can have many entries per contact; CNAME names can't have others.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Apex direct, www aliased to CDN, api round-robin.

code.text:
example.com.       300 IN A     203.0.113.10
example.com.       300 IN AAAA  2001:db8::10
www.example.com.   300 IN CNAME d123.cloudfront.net.
api.example.com.   60  IN A     203.0.113.20
api.example.com.   60  IN A     203.0.113.21

check.q: Why can't you put a CNAME at the zone apex?
check.a: The apex must have SOA and NS records, and a CNAME can't coexist with any other record at the same name.

specialized-records-mx-txt-and-srv.core: MX records list mail servers for a domain with priorities (lower is preferred). TXT records hold arbitrary text, used for SPF (allowed senders), DKIM keys, DMARC policy and domain ownership verification. SRV records give service location (priority, weight, port, target) for protocols like SIP, XMPP and Kerberos. CAA restricts which certificate authorities may issue for the domain.

first_principles.problem: Marketing emails land in spam because SPF and DMARC records are missing.
truths: Domains need to prove ownership and policies.
Services may run on non-standard ports.

analogy.title: Building directory signs
analogy.story: 'Deliveries: loading dock B, then C' (MX); notices on the board (TXT); 'IT help: room 4, extension 22' (SRV).
analogy.breaks: Notice boards aren't machine-parsed; SPF/DMARC syntax is strict.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Mail authenticated, SIP discoverable, cert issuance restricted.

code.text:
example.com.            MX  10 mx1.mailhost.net.
example.com.            MX  20 mx2.mailhost.net.
example.com.            TXT "v=spf1 include:_spf.mailhost.net -all"
_dmarc.example.com.     TXT "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com"
_sip._tcp.example.com.  SRV 10 60 5060 sip1.example.com.
example.com.            CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"

check.q: What does a lower MX priority number mean?
check.a: Higher preference; senders try the lowest-numbered MX first.

infrastructure-records-ns-and-soa.core: NS records delegate a zone to its authoritative name servers; the parent zone (for example .com) holds matching NS and glue records pointing to them. The SOA record defines zone metadata: primary server, admin email, serial number, refresh and retry timers for secondaries, and the negative-caching TTL. Mismatched NS at parent and child, or forgotten serial bumps, cause subtle outages.

first_principles.problem: After migrating DNS providers, half of users still hit the old provider because the registrar's NS records weren't updated.
truths: Delegation is set at the parent.
derivation: Bump **SOA serial** on changes (if using AXFR).

analogy.title: Official land registry pointing to the local office
analogy.story: The national registry says which local office holds the deeds; if it points to the old office, people go there.
analogy.breaks: Registries update slowly by post; NS changes depend on TTLs.

code.text:
dig NS example.com +short                   # what the zone says
dig NS example.com @a.gtld-servers.net      # what the parent delegates
dig SOA example.com +short
# ns1.provider.net. hostmaster.example.com. 2026101801 7200 3600 1209600 300

check.q: Where must NS changes be made to migrate DNS providers?
check.a: At the parent zone via the registrar (and in the zone itself), otherwise resolvers keep being sent to the old servers.

ttl-and-caching-why-dns-changes-arent-in.core: Every DNS record has a TTL in seconds telling resolvers how long to cache it. Changing a record only takes effect for a client once its resolver's cached copy expires, so with a TTL of 86400 that could be a day. Some clients, OS caches and Java's default caching ignore or extend TTLs. Lower TTLs in advance of planned changes, and remember negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached too.

first_principles.problem: A failover to a new IP takes hours because the record had a 24-hour TTL.
truths: Caching trades freshness for load and speed.

analogy.title: Printed menus vs a chalkboard
analogy.story: Printed menus (long TTL) are cheap but slow to update; a chalkboard (short TTL) changes instantly but needs constant attention.
analogy.breaks: Menus can be collected; caches only expire.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows how long the old answer will persist.

code.text:
dig api.example.com @1.1.1.1 | grep -A1 'ANSWER SECTION'
# api.example.com. 2873 IN A 203.0.113.20   ← seconds remaining in cache

check.q: How should you prepare a DNS record for a planned IP migration?
check.a: Lower its TTL at least one old-TTL period in advance, make the change, then raise the TTL again.

advanced-concept-split-horizon-dns.core: Split-horizon DNS returns different answers for the same name depending on who asks. Internal clients get private IPs (10.x) and external clients get public ones, or internal-only names exist only inside. It's implemented with views (BIND), private hosted zones (Route 53) or conditional forwarding. It keeps internal topology hidden but makes debugging harder, because 'what does this resolve to?' depends on where you are.

first_principles.problem: Internal users hairpin through the public load balancer for an internal app, adding latency and egress cost.

analogy.title: A building with an internal and public directory
analogy.story: Staff see office extensions; visitors see the main reception number for the same department.
analogy.breaks: Visitors can't accidentally see the staff directory; misconfigured views can leak.

code.text:
# from inside VPC
dig +short app.acme.com     # 10.0.2.15
# from internet
dig +short app.acme.com @1.1.1.1   # 203.0.113.30

check.q: What's a common debugging pitfall with split-horizon DNS?
check.a: Results depend on which resolver you query, so engineers testing from a laptop vs inside the VPC see different answers.

advanced-concept-anycast-dns.core: Major DNS providers announce the same IP addresses via BGP from dozens or hundreds of locations (anycast). Queries reach the topologically nearest instance, giving low latency, automatic failover (a dead site withdraws its route), and DDoS absorption across sites. Root servers, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8 and Route 53 all use anycast; UDP's statelessness makes DNS an ideal fit.

first_principles.problem: A single-location DNS server makes lookups slow for users in other continents and is easily DDoSed.
truths: BGP routes to the nearest announcement.
DNS over UDP is mostly stateless.

analogy.title: One emergency number everywhere
analogy.story: Dial 112 anywhere in Europe and the nearest centre answers.
analogy.breaks: Phone routing is geographic; BGP 'nearest' is topological, not always geographic.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Different locations see different PoP IDs for the same IP.

code.text:
dig @1.1.1.1 id.server CH TXT +short
# "FRA"   ← Frankfurt PoP served this query
dig @k.root-servers.net hostname.bind CH TXT +short

check.q: Why is DNS particularly well suited to anycast?
check.a: Queries are short, mostly stateless UDP exchanges, so route changes mid-session rarely break anything.

security-dnssec-and-dns-over-https.core: Classic DNS is unauthenticated and unencrypted. DNSSEC adds authenticity: zones sign records (RRSIG), publish keys (DNSKEY), and parents vouch for children (DS records) in a chain of trust up to the root, so validating resolvers reject forged answers. Encrypted DNS (DoH, DoT) adds privacy between client and resolver. They solve different problems: integrity versus confidentiality.

first_principles.problem: A cache-poisoning attack redirects a bank's domain to a phishing server for users of one ISP.
truths: Trust must chain to a known anchor.

analogy.title: A sealed, signed letter vs an opaque envelope
analogy.story: A signature proves who sent it (DNSSEC); an opaque envelope hides what it says (DoH). You may want both.
analogy.breaks: Signatures on letters are rarely checked; validating resolvers check every answer.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Proves answers are signed and validated.

code.text:
dig +dnssec example.com A | grep -E 'RRSIG|flags'
# flags: qr rd ra ad;   ← 'ad' = authenticated data (validated)
delv example.com A
# ; fully validated

check.a: No, it only signs records for authenticity; DoH/DoT provide encryption.
